43120: Eden (Gen 3), Moses' staff turned to a snake (Exod 4:3; Exod 7:10-12), fiery serpents (Num 21:6), wine biting like a serpent (Prov 23:32), Leviathan the twisting serpent (Isa 27:1), the serpent eating dust in the new creation (Isa 65:25).
43121: Brood of vipers (Matt 3:7; Matt 23:33), bread or a snake (Matt 7:10), the lifted serpent (John 3:14), Paul's viper (Acts 28:3), the ancient serpent (Rev 12:9).
43122: The fiery serpents (seraphim) of Num 21:6 share a word with the seraphim of Isa 6:2; some scholars think the seraphim were pictured as winged serpents, others disagree. Snake-handling as a test of faith rests on a textually uncertain verse.
43126: The eagle in the Bible is a symbol of strength, speed, care and renewal, especially in 'they shall mount up with wings as eagles'. The Hebrew word nesher often means the griffon vulture, so some passages that say 'eagle' picture birds gathering at carcasses.
43128: God bore Israel 'on eagles' wings', like a bird stirring and carrying its young.
43130: Those who wait on the LORD rise up with fresh strength.
43131: Swift invading armies and proud kingdoms
43132: Babylon is a great eagle; Edom nests among the stars but will be brought down.
43134: Many translations now say 'vultures'. Jesus' saying means judgement will be as obvious as birds circling a body. A Roman-eagle reading (the legions' standards) is sometimes proposed; it is debated.
43135: The woman of Rev 12 receives eagle's wings to flee to the wilderness, echoing the exodus. Church tradition (Jerome, Augustine) assigned the eagle to John's soaring Gospel.
43136: Unclean bird (Lev 11:13), the exodus image (Exod 19:4), Saul and Jonathan swifter than eagles (2 Sam 1:23), Babylon as an eagle (Ezek 17:3), winged lion (Dan 7:4).
43137: Vultures at the carcass (Matt 24:28), the fourth living creature (Rev 4:7), an eagle crying woe (Rev 8:13), eagle's wings for the woman (Rev 12:14).
43138: The legend that the eagle renews youth by flying near the sun and plunging into water comes from medieval bestiaries, not from Ps 103:5.
43140: Oxen were the farmer's strength, pulling ploughs and carts, and bulls were the most costly sacrifice. The ox stands for labour and strength, the bull for sacrifice and for power that could become an idol, as with the golden calf.
43142: 'Do not muzzle the ox while it treads grain.' Paul applies it to paying gospel workers.
43144: Bulls were offered for the priest's sin and on the Day of Atonement; Hebrews contrasts them with Christ's self-offering.
43146: The golden calf and Jeroboam's calves at Bethel and Dan. Bulls were common symbols for gods like Baal; some scholars think the calves were pedestals for an invisible God rather than images of him.
43147: Tradition linked the ox (or calf) with Luke, whose Gospel begins with a priest offering in the temple.
43149: 'The ox knows its owner, but Israel does not know.' This verse later inspired the ox and donkey in nativity scenes.
43150: Goring ox laws (Exod 21:28), twelve bronze oxen under the sea (1 Kgs 7:25), Elisha ploughing with twelve yoke (1 Kgs 19:19), lion eating straw like the ox (Isa 11:7).
43151: Rescuing an ox on the sabbath (Luke 14:5), the fatted calf (Luke 15:23), the yoke (Matt 11:29-30), muzzled ox (1 Cor 9:9), calf-faced creature (Rev 4:7).
43152: The law not to plough with ox and donkey together (Deut 22:10) is often linked to 'unequally yoked' (2 Cor 6:14); Paul does not cite it, so the link is a likely echo at best.
43155: In Bible times horses were war machines, not farm animals. They stand for military might, which Israel was warned not to trust. In visions, coloured horses carry God's judgements through the earth, and Christ returns on a white horse.
43157: 'Some trust in chariots and some in horses.' Kings were not to multiply horses.
43159: Chariots and horses of fire surround Elisha.
43160: Agents of judgement through the earth
43161: Revelation's four horsemen draw on Zechariah. The first rider on a white horse is debated: Christ or the gospel's advance (some Fathers), or a conqueror and false messiah who imitates Christ (many modern readers).
43163: The rider called Faithful and True, the Word of God, wins with the sword from his mouth.
43165: Bit and bridle picture discipline of speech and stubbornness.
43166: Pharaoh's horses in the sea (Exod 15:1), Solomon's horse trade (1 Kgs 10:28), the warhorse of Job (Job 39:19-25), renouncing horses (Hos 14:3), the king who cuts off the war-horse (Zech 9:10).
43167: Bits in horses' mouths (Jas 3:3), the horsemen (Rev 6), demonic cavalry (Rev 9:16-17), the white horse of Christ (Rev 19:11).
43168: The contrast between horse and donkey matters: the messianic king of Zech 9:9-10 rides a donkey and removes the war-horse.
43170: Donkeys were the everyday working animal and could also be the mount of leaders in peacetime. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah's picture of a king who comes humbly and brings peace. Balaam's donkey famously sees the angel and speaks.
43172: Matthew has a donkey and a colt; many take this as reading Zechariah's poetic parallel literally, others think two animals were really present. Either way the king comes in peace, not on a war-horse.
43174: Leaders rode donkeys; Solomon was crowned on David's mule. So the donkey is humble compared to a war-horse, but not shameful.
43176: Balaam's donkey sees the angel the prophet cannot see.
43178: Binding a donkey to a vine pictures such plenty that no one minds the donkey eating the grapes. Many read it as messianic, echoed in Zech 9:9.
43179: Abraham's donkey to Moriah (Gen 22:3), firstborn donkeys redeemed with a lamb (Exod 13:13), Saul looking for lost donkeys (1 Sam 9:3), Samson's jawbone (Judg 15:15), the burial of a donkey as disgrace (Jer 22:19).
43180: Triumphal entry (Matt 21:5), untying a donkey on the sabbath (Luke 13:15), Balaam's donkey (2 Pet 2:16). The donkey at the nativity is tradition (from Isa 1:3), not in the Gospels.
43181: The ancient slur that Jews or Christians worshipped a donkey (reported by Tertullian and seen in the Alexamenos graffito) is a pagan insult, not a biblical symbol.
43184: Israel was a nation of shepherds, so God's people are pictured as sheep and their leaders as shepherds. God is the true shepherd, bad kings are condemned as false shepherds, and Jesus calls himself the Good Shepherd who lays down his life.
43186: Kings across the ancient Near East were called shepherds; Israel applies the title first to God.
43187: Leaders as shepherds, good and bad
43188: Leaders who feed themselves instead of the flock are judged. Elders are told to shepherd willingly. 'Pastor' comes from the Latin for shepherd.
43190: Jesus claims the role God promised for himself and for a coming David. He knows, calls, gathers and dies for the sheep.
43191: People who are lost or helpless
43192: Sheep without a shepherd wander and scatter.
43193: Sheep and goats at the judgement
43194: Shepherds separated mixed flocks at night. See 'goat' for the point and its limits.
43195: Abel, the patriarchs, Moses and David as shepherds (Gen 4:2; Exod 3:1; 1 Sam 16:11), the struck shepherd and scattered sheep (Zech 13:7), the coming ruler who shepherds (Mic 5:4).
43196: Shepherds at the nativity (Luke 2:8), the lost sheep (Luke 15:4), the Good Shepherd (John 10), 'feed my sheep' (John 21:17), the Lamb who shepherds (Rev 7:17).
43197: Sheep imagery is about dependence on a good shepherd, not a call to unthinking passivity; the same texts judge abusive leaders harshly.
43201: Goats were ordinary flock animals and acceptable sacrifices. On the Day of Atonement one goat was sacrificed and another, the scapegoat, carried Israel's sins into the wilderness. In Jesus' parable, goats on the left stand for those who failed to care for 'the least of these'.
43203: One goat is 'for the LORD', the other 'for Azazel'. Azazel is debated: a wilderness demon, a place name, or 'the goat that goes away'. Christians see both goats fulfilled in Christ's death and removal of sin.
43205: Male goats were regular sin offerings; Hebrews says such blood cannot finally remove sin.
43207: The sheep and goats are judged by how they treated Christ's 'least' brothers and sisters. Who the 'least' are (all needy people or Christian messengers) is debated.
43209: The he-goat is the king of Greece, generally identified with Alexander the Great.
43211: Jacob deceives Isaac with goat-skins; years later his sons deceive him with a goat's blood on Joseph's coat.
43212: Passover could be a lamb or goat (Exod 12:5), goat-hair curtains (Exod 26:7), goat-demons or 'satyrs' (Lev 17:7; Isa 13:21), the beloved's hair like goats (Song 4:1), Ezekiel judging between rams and goats (Ezek 34:17).
43213: Sheep and goats (Matt 25:32), the older brother's complaint about never getting a goat (Luke 15:29), blood of goats (Heb 9:12).
43214: Goats are not inherently evil; they were clean animals and valid sacrifices. The modern devil-with-goat-horns imagery comes from later art, not from Scripture.
43216: The wolf is the enemy of the flock. Scripture uses it for violent rulers, false teachers who come 'in sheep's clothing', and the dangers disciples face. In the age to come, the wolf will live peacefully with the lamb.
43218: Wolves in sheep's clothing; savage wolves entering the flock; officials like wolves tearing prey.
43219: A hostile world for the disciples
43220: Disciples are sent as sheep among wolves; the hired hand flees when the wolf comes.
43222: Whether this is literal peace among animals or a picture of peace between enemies (or both) is debated.
43224: Benjamin is 'a ravenous wolf', a warrior tribe. Some Fathers applied it to Paul, a Benjaminite who once 'ravaged' the church (Phil 3:5); tradition.
43225: Benjamin (Gen 49:27), wolves of the evening (Hab 1:8; Zeph 3:3), a wolf destroying the disobedient (Jer 5:6), the wolf with the lamb (Isa 11:6).
43226: False prophets (Matt 7:15), sheep among wolves (Luke 10:3), the hireling and the wolf (John 10:12), Paul's warning to Ephesian elders (Acts 20:29).
43227: 'Wolf' was used for real dangers; using it to dismiss anyone who disagrees with us turns a warning into a weapon.
43229: In the Bible most dogs were half-wild scavengers, not pets, so 'dog' was usually an insult for someone contemptible, unclean or dangerous. Yet the Canaanite woman turns Jesus' 'little dogs' saying into a plea of faith.
43231: 'Am I a dog?' 'A dead dog' was a strong phrase of self-abasement or insult.
43232: Scavengers as a sign of judgement
43233: Being eaten by dogs was the worst dishonour. In Ps 22 enemies surround like dogs.
43235: A dog returning to its vomit pictures people going back to what harmed them.
43236: Outsiders, and how they receive grace
43237: Jewish speech sometimes called Gentiles dogs. Jesus' 'little dogs' saying and the woman's reply lead to praise of her faith. Readers debate whether Jesus was testing her, voicing a common view to overturn it, or genuinely persuaded.
43238: Those excluded from the holy city
43239: Paul turns the insult on Christian circumcision-teachers. In Deut 23:18 'dog' may refer to a male cult prostitute; the meaning is debated.
43240: Not a dog moving its tongue at the exodus (Exod 11:7), unclean meat thrown to dogs (Exod 22:31), Gideon's men lapping like dogs (Judg 7:5), silent watchdogs as lazy prophets (Isa 56:10), a living dog better than a dead lion (Eccl 9:4).
43241: Do not give what is holy to dogs (Matt 7:6), dogs licking Lazarus' sores (Luke 16:21), the Canaanite woman (Matt 15:27), 'beware of dogs' (Phil 3:2), outside the city (Rev 22:15).
43242: A friendly dog appears in the deuterocanonical book of Tobit, travelling with Tobias. The Bible's negative uses reflect street dogs of the time, not a judgement on dogs today.
43245: Pigs were unclean under the law of Moses, so they became a symbol of what is unclean or of the far, Gentile world. In Jesus' teaching, the prodigal son feeding pigs has hit bottom, and the demons sent into a herd of pigs show that 'Legion' is defeated.
43247: Eating pork marked rebellion in Isaiah. Under the Seleucids, Jews were pressured to eat pork and some died refusing (told in 2 Maccabees 6-7).
43249: A Jewish son feeding a Gentile's pigs, longing for their food, has lost everything.
43250: Unable to value what is holy
43251: Pearls before swine; a gold ring in a pig's snout.
43253: Unclean spirits go into unclean animals in Gentile territory and are drowned. Some scholars note the boar was the emblem of the Roman Tenth Legion stationed in the region and see a jab at Rome in 'Legion'; that is speculative.
43255: Mark comments that Jesus 'declared all foods clean'; Peter's vision includes unclean animals. Christians debate how and when food laws ceased to apply, but most agree they do not bind Gentile believers.
43256: Food laws (Lev 11:7), the wild boar ravaging God's vine (Ps 80:13), pig's blood in idolatrous worship (Isa 66:3).
43257: Pearls before swine (Matt 7:6), the Gerasene pigs (Mark 5:13), the prodigal (Luke 15:15), the washed pig back in the mud (2 Pet 2:22).
43258: The point of the pig is ritual status, not hygiene. The 'health reasons' explanation for food laws is a modern idea that the text does not give.
43260: Ravens were unclean scavengers, yet God feeds them and uses them to feed Elijah. Jesus points to the ravens to show that God cares for those who seem least deserving, so his people need not worry.
43262: Jesus: they neither sow nor reap, yet God feeds them. How much more you.
43264: Unclean birds bring bread and meat to the prophet. A few scholars repoint the Hebrew to read 'Arabians' instead of 'ravens'; most keep ravens.
43266: The raven goes to and fro and does not return, unlike the dove. Fathers sometimes read the raven as the unclean or unrepentant; tradition.
43268: Ravens inhabit ruins and peck out the eyes of the scornful.
43269: Unclean bird (Lev 11:15; Deut 14:14), Noah's raven (Gen 8:7), Elijah's ravens (1 Kgs 17:6), ravens in ruined Edom (Isa 34:11), hair black as a raven (Song 5:11).
43270: Only Luke 12:24 (Matthew says 'birds of the air', Matt 6:26).
43271: That ravens are unclean sharpens the point of providence; it does not make them symbols of evil in every text.
43273: Fish were a staple food around Galilee, and several disciples were fishermen. Jesus calls them to 'fish for people', multiplies fish, and eats fish after rising. Early Christians used the Greek word for fish, ICHTHYS, as an acrostic for 'Jesus Christ, God's Son, Saviour'.
43275: In Jeremiah fishers gather for judgement; Jesus turns the image toward gathering people into the kingdom.
43277: A dragnet gathers every kind; good and bad are separated at the end.
43279: Feeding the crowds; breakfast on the shore; Ezekiel's river makes the Dead Sea teem with fish.
43281: Jesus eats fish to show he is not a ghost.
43283: The letters stand for Iesous Christos Theou Yios Soter. Tertullian (*On Baptism* 1) calls Christians little fish after the great Fish, and Augustine (*City of God* 18.23) discusses the acrostic. This is early church tradition, not biblical symbolism.
43284: Creation of sea creatures (Gen 1:21), the great fish of Jonah (Jonah 1:17), clean and unclean fish (Lev 11:9-12), fish dying in the Nile plague (Exod 7:21), people caught like fish (Hab 1:14-15; Eccl 9:12).
43285: Fishermen disciples (Mark 1:16-17), feedings (Mark 6:41), the coin in the fish (Matt 17:27), the sign of Jonah (Matt 12:40), 153 fish (John 21:11).
43286: The idea that 'the sign of the fish' was a secret code drawn in the sand during persecution is a popular story with little ancient evidence. The Philistine god Dagon is often said to be a fish-god, but most scholars now link the name to grain.
43288: Locust swarms could strip a land bare, so they were a terrifying image of judgement and invading armies. Yet locusts were also clean food: John the Baptist ate locusts and wild honey. Revelation's locusts from the abyss are demonic and nightmarish.
43290: The eighth plague; covenant curse; Solomon's prayer for relief.
43292: Joel's locusts are either a real plague described as an army, a real army described as locusts, or both stages. Scholars debate.
43294: 'I will restore the years the locust has eaten.'
43296: Locusts with human faces and scorpion tails, led by Abaddon/Apollyon. Modern attempts to identify them as helicopters or aircraft are speculative.
43298: Most scholars take these as insects (permitted food). The 'locust bean' or carob pod reading is a later suggestion.
43299: Plague in Egypt (Exod 10), clean insects (Lev 11:22), spies 'like grasshoppers' (Num 13:33), Midianite hordes (Judg 6:5), Amos' vision (Amos 7:1), locusts with no king who still march in ranks (Prov 30:27).
43300: John's diet (Matt 3:4; Mark 1:6) and the fifth trumpet (Rev 9:3-11).
43301: Locusts are a vivid image, but not every swarm or pest outbreak today is a 'sign'. Context in Joel and Revelation is judgement calling for repentance.
43303: Leviathan is a great sea creature in Hebrew poetry. Sometimes it seems to be a real animal (a crocodile or whale) that only God can tame; sometimes it is a many-headed chaos monster that God crushes. Either way the point is God's total mastery over the most frightening powers.
43304: A creature only God can master
43305: In Job, God asks if Job can catch Leviathan with a hook. Many identify it with the crocodile; others see a mythic beast described with real animal features. In Ps 104 it is God's creature playing in the sea.
43306: Chaos and evil defeated by God
43307: God crushed Leviathan's heads; he will slay 'Leviathan the twisting serpent'. Texts from Ugarit describe a seven-headed sea serpent called Litan with very similar wording, so Israel used a known image to declare that the LORD, not Baal, rules the sea.
43309: In Ps 74 crushing Leviathan is linked to the Red Sea; Egypt is elsewhere a sea-dragon.
43310: Background to Revelation's dragon and sea beast
43311: The many-headed dragon and the beast from the sea draw on this imagery. The term Leviathan itself is not used in the NT.
43313: Not named; its imagery informs the dragon and sea beast of Revelation (Rev 12-13). Rev 21:1 'no more sea' completes the defeat of chaos.
43314: Reading Leviathan as a surviving dinosaur or sea reptile is a modern young-earth creationist proposal and is not the scholarly consensus. Later Jewish writings (2 Baruch, rabbinic texts) imagined Leviathan served at the messianic banquet; that is tradition.
43317: Behemoth appears in God's speech to Job as a massive land creature, 'the first of the works of God', that only its Maker can approach with a sword. The name means something like 'the Beast' or 'the super-beast'. Most identify it with the hippopotamus; others see a mythic creature.
43319: God shows Job a creature far beyond human control to humble him and to show God's wise rule even over the wild.
43320: Identity: hippopotamus, elephant, or mythic beast
43321: It lies under lotus plants in the reeds and is unafraid of a raging river, which fits the hippo. 'Tail like a cedar' (Job 40:17) is hard for the hippo; some read 'tail' as a euphemism, others as poetic exaggeration. Later Jewish texts (*1 Enoch* 60:7-8) pair a land-monster Behemoth with sea-monster Leviathan.
43323: Some young-earth creationists identify Behemoth with a sauropod because of the 'tail like a cedar'. Most biblical scholars do not accept this.
43324: Only Job 40:15-24 as a proper name; the ordinary plural 'beasts' (behemot) appears often, as in Ps 73:22 ('I was a beast before you').
43326: Job's point is not zoology. The creature humbles human pride and shows God's sovereign care over things that terrify us.
43328: The Hebrew tannin can mean a large sea creature, a snake or a sea monster. In poetry it stands for chaos and for proud empires like Egypt and Babylon. In Revelation the great red dragon is Satan, who wars against the woman and her child and gives power to the beast.
43329: The dragon is explicitly identified as 'that ancient serpent, called the devil and Satan'. Seven heads and ten horns link him to the beasts he empowers.
43331: Pharaoh is the great dragon in the Nile; Nebuchadnezzar swallowed Judah like a dragon. Rahab here is a sea-monster name, not Rahab of Jericho.
43333: God created the great tanninim; they praise him. Even the monsters are creatures.
43335: The LORD slays the dragon in the sea; the faithful trample it.
43336: Sea creatures (Gen 1:21), Aaron's staff becomes a tannin (Exod 7:9-10), venom of dragons (Deut 32:33), Egypt and Babylon (Ezek 29:3; Jer 51:34).
43337: Only Revelation: the red dragon (Rev 12:3), its gift of power to the beast (Rev 13:2-4), frog-like spirits from its mouth (Rev 16:13), bound for a thousand years (Rev 20:2).
43338: The KJV uses 'dragons' for jackals in several prophets (e.g. Isa 13:22; Jer 9:11; Mic 1:8) by confusing two similar Hebrew words (tan, jackal; tannin, sea monster). Modern versions correct this. 'Bel and the Dragon' is an addition to Daniel in the deuterocanon.
43340: In Daniel 7 four monstrous beasts rise from the sea and stand for world empires, until 'one like a son of man' receives the kingdom. Revelation 13 combines their features into one beast from the sea, aided by a second beast from the land. The beast is political power that demands worship. Who it refers to has been one of the most debated questions in Christian history.
43342: The angel explains the beasts as kings or kingdoms. Traditional reading: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome. Most critical scholars: Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece (ending with Antiochus IV as the little horn). Both views have able defenders.
43343: Beastly power versus the human Son of Man
43344: Empires are beasts; God's kingdom is given to a human figure and to the saints. Jesus applies the Son of Man to himself.
43346: Seven hills and seven kings fit Rome. The healed death-wound may echo the legend that Nero would return (reported by Tacitus and Suetonius). Widely held by modern scholars as at least the first reference.
43348: A final world ruler before Christ returns. Held by many evangelicals and dispensationalists; also by some early Fathers.
43349: The papacy, or recurring tyranny (historicist and idealist readings)
43350: Many Reformers identified the beast or Antichrist with the papacy; this view has largely faded and is rejected by Catholics. Idealists see a pattern repeating in every age when the state claims divine honours.
43351: Daniel's four beasts (Dan 7), ram and goat (Dan 8:20-21), with background in the sea monster imagery of Leviathan.
43352: Revelation's sea beast and land beast or false prophet (Rev 13:1; Rev 13:11; Rev 16:13), the beast from the abyss (Rev 11:7; Rev 17:8), its defeat (Rev 19:20; Rev 20:10).
43353: Each generation has found 'the beast' in its own enemies. A wise reading notices what the beast does (deceives, demands worship, persecutes, controls trade) and resists those patterns, rather than confidently naming one person.
43355: The grapevine was one of Israel's main crops, so Israel itself is pictured as God's vine or vineyard, which he planted and tended but which gave bad fruit. Jesus says, 'I am the true vine'; his followers live by staying joined to him. Sitting under one's own vine pictures peace and security.
43357: God brought a vine out of Egypt; he looked for good grapes and found wild ones.
43359: Jesus takes Israel's identity on himself: as the faithful vine he gives life to branches who abide in him. Whether 'taken away' branches (John 15:2) are lost believers or never-true disciples is debated.
